authors: Vittoria Magrelli; Roy Suddaby; Trevor Israelsen; Emanuela Rondi; Alfredo De Massis

title: The Future of Entrepreneurship Research Includes Online Panel Data—If Used Correctly
authors: Jeffrey M. Pollack; J. Jeffrey Gish; Timothy L. Michaelis; Jeni L. Burnette; David J. Scheaf; Jon C. Carr; Nicholas A. Smith
affiliations: Management, Innovation, and Entrepreneurship, NC State University, Raleigh, NC, USA; Whitman School of Management, Syracuse University, NY, USA; Department of Psychology, NC State University, Raleigh, NC, USA; Hankamer School of Business, Baylor University, Waco, TX, USA; Northern Illinois University, DeKalb, IL, USA
abstract: As online panel data (OPD) become more widely used across the behavioral sciences, editors, reviewers, and researchers in entrepreneurship are asking whether it has a legitimate place in our field. We believe the answer is yes—provided three conditions are met. First, the online panel’s participants and definition of entrepreneur must match the research question. Second, studies must incorporate best practices for sample verification. Third, generalizability must be explicitly addressed as part of the study (or set of studies). If researchers do these things, OPD can meaningfully advance both theory and practice in entrepreneurship research. That said, real questions remain. What kinds of studies are suitable for OPD? Who are these respondents, and are they who they say they are? Are they human, and are they entrepreneurs as commonly defined in the literature? Our recommendations and checklist aim to enable entrepreneurship researchers to answer these questions and make informed choices when collecting data and publishing results using OPD.

title: Strategy as a theory of change
authors: Sergio G. Lazzarini; Todd R. Zenger; Teppo Felin
affiliations: Insper São Paulo Brazil; David Eccles School of Business University of Utah Salt Lake City Utah USA
abstract: Abstract Research Summary The theory‐based view argues that a strategist's task is to develop a theory to move the organization to an improved future state. Focusing on theorizing as a thought process of model creation, we propose a framework to specify hypothetical causal links and analyze their structure as a directed graph connecting inputs, activities, and indicators of problem resolution. We then propose a set of metrics operationalizing key theory attributes: complexity, equifinality, interdependence, and circularity. We discuss the strategic relevance of these attributes in terms of a theory's ability to promote comprehensive problem resolution as well as implement, evaluate, and replicate the proposed solution. Our work represents a step toward operationalizing model creation in the theory‐based view and informs the design of strategic theories of change. Managerial Summary Strategists often theorize how to move their organizations toward an improved performance state. Yet most strategic analysis tools describe the organization's external environment or the internal components of its business model, without precisely specifying forward‐looking interventions that might cause the desired changes. In this paper, we represent strategic theories as a chain of causal interventions—inputs and activities that address relevant problems and lead to desirable outcomes. We propose a structured framework that helps managers develop theories and measure key attributes that influence comprehensive problem resolution and the ability to implement, evaluate, and replicate the proposed interventions. In this sense, our work helps managers mentally create their strategic theories and assess their usefulness as a roadmap to superior performance.

title: Who Benefits from Citizenship? Varying Effects of Naturalization Decisions in the Early-Twentieth-Century United States
authors: Peter Catron; Nathan I. Hoffmann; Mingze Li
affiliations: University of Washington, USA; Emory University, USA
abstract: Citizenship acquisition is widely viewed as a mechanism for improving economic outcomes, yet little is known about whether its benefits are distributed evenly. This article examines the varied returns to naturalization in the early-twentieth-century United States, assessing whether naturalization uniformly benefits all immigrants or is especially impactful for those already positioned to profit. Using naturalization records from New York City’s Southern District in the early 1900s, we construct a novel historical dataset for 1,947 immigrants who declared their intent to naturalize. By linking these records to U.S. census data from 1920, 1930, and 1940, we are able to observe immigrants’ characteristics at the point when they make naturalization decisions and to track their outcomes over time. Our findings reveal that immigrants who completed the naturalization process attained significantly higher occupational status than those who initiated but did not complete naturalization. In addition, citizenship is most transformative for those facing the greatest disadvantages. Additional analyses corroborate these findings in linked full-count census data for the entire United States. Citizenship confers occupational advantages not only through formal rights but as a resource that enables claims-making in the labor market, with greater returns to less advantaged immigrants.

title: Dueling Political Fictions and Public Administration and Democracy in an Era of Populism and Authoritarian Impulses
authors: Michael W. Spicer
affiliations: Cleveland State University Cleveland Ohio USA
abstract: ABSTRACT The political fictions used in political discourse, during the English Civil War period, remain relevant to contemporary public policy and administration. Mainstream public administration discourse has too often employed the fiction of a singular and unbounded popular sovereignty that emerged during this period, leaving public administration ill‐equipped to deal with the authoritarian impulses of contemporary populist governments. What is needed in public administration discourse, in dealing with these authoritarian impulses, is not an ethic of administrative neutrality, such as has traditionally dominated much of our field, but an ethic of constitutionalism that draws on the fiction of the individual that was also articulated during the English Civil War period by the English Levellers and subsequently by the founders of the American Constitution.

Demand for Research and the Composition of Scientific Response: Intellectual Distance, Research Productivity, and Research Outcomes
authors: Jino Lu
affiliations: Washington University in St Louis, Olin Business School, St. Louis, Missouri, United States
abstract: When demand for research in a domain increases, scientific progress depends not only on whether more research is produced, but also on which scientists produce that research. This distinction is especially important in emerging domains, where technological trajectories remain uncertain and progress often requires the generation and integration of heterogeneous scientific knowledge. This study examines how academic scientists respond when demand for research increases in a domain and what research outcomes they produce within that domain. Empirically, I exploit the Zero Emission Vehicle (ZEV) mandate, which led to an unanticipated increase in demand for electric vehicle (EV) research. I find that scientists became more likely to produce EV research after the mandate. However, this response varied systematically across scientists: as intellectual distance from the EV domain increased, more-productive scientists were less responsive than less-productive scientists. Yet among scientists who produced EV research, the research outcomes of scientists from more distant domains were associated with greater novelty, while those of more-productive scientists from more distant domains were associated with greater scientific impact and greater use in downstream EV inventions. These findings suggest that increased demand for research shapes not only the volume of scientific activity in a domain, but also the composition of scientists who produce that research.

title: Willingness to Compete in Dirty Competitions
authors: Thomas Buser; Sahar Sangi
affiliations: University of Amsterdam and Tinbergen Institute, 1018WB Amsterdam, Netherlands
abstract: Competitive environments often leave room for “dirty” practices such as sabotage, retaliation, or dishonesty. We use an online experiment to document aggregate levels and individual differences in the willingness to engage in dirty competition and in the willingness to enter competitions where the opponent may play dirty. We then use the experimental data to validate a set of survey questions that capture willingness to engage in dirty competition above general willingness to compete. We elicit these questions in a representative survey panel and show that willingness to engage in dirty competition is a strong predictor of holding a management or supervisory position and of working in the private—versus the public—sector, but also of worse self-esteem, worse social relationships, and increased feelings of guilt and shame. Men, younger people, and lower-educated people are on average more willing to engage in dirty competition. This paper was accepted by Dorothea Kübler, behavioral economics and decision analysis. title: Contest or Contract: Assessing the Effectiveness of Contests in Online Labor Markets
authors: Jason Chan; Jiahui Mo; Tingting Nian; Nila Zhang
affiliations: Carlson School of Management, University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, Minnesota 55455; Poole College of Management, North Carolina State University, Raleigh, North Carolina 27695; The Paul Merage School of Business, University of California, Irvine, California 92697; School of Management, Fudan University, Shanghai 200433, China
abstract: Online labor markets have become increasingly popular among companies seeking global access to workers. Some platforms have adopted a contest-based scheme, allowing employers to review multiple submissions before selecting the best one. This practice raises a crucial question: Given a predefined budget, should employers choose a contest or contract scheme for tasks? This study examines the comparative effectiveness of contests versus contracts in achieving better job outcomes, focusing on design tasks characterized by high uncertainty. Using a comprehensive data set from a leading online labor market, we employ multiple empirical strategies, combined with machine learning and text mining techniques, to examine the impact of compensation schemes on job quality. Our results suggest that contract-based jobs yield better performance than contests in the context of ideation tasks. Further analysis, such as examining image similarity among pairwise solutions within a task, identifies “copying” behaviors as a key mechanism undermining the effectiveness of contests. In the public setting of contests, workers can observe others’ submissions and revise their own, leading to imitation rather than innovation. As competition intensity increases, workers have weaker incentives to exert effort, reducing solution quality. Consequently, the negative incentive effects in contests outweigh both the potential positive incentive and parallel effects. Moreover, although information availability can enhance work quality, contests inherently offer limited informational advantages compared with contracts. Taken together, our findings suggest that contract-based schemes are more effective than contests for design tasks, offering important implications for both employers and platform designers in online labor markets. This paper was accepted by Karan Girotra, operations management. Funding: N. Zhang acknowledges the support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72302053]. title: Multitype Information Acquisition in a Strategic Trading Model
authors: Hui Ou-Yang; Weili Wu; Xingtan Zhang
affiliations: Department of Finance, Cheung Kong Graduate School of Business, Beijing 100010, China; School of Finance, Central University of Finance and Economics, Beijing 100081, China
abstract: We analyze information acquisition in a strategic trading model with multidimensional uncertainties. Our main result is that the equilibrium can exhibit multiplicity because of the integer nature of the number of informed traders and the strategic interactions across different types of informed traders. We show that the number of equilibria can be arbitrarily large. Moreover, asymmetric equilibria can arise even in symmetric settings. As information costs rise, fewer traders acquire information, yet prices can become more informative. These results shed light on the instability of financial markets and yield testable empirical predictions. This paper was accepted by Lukas Schmid, finance. title: Inflexibility and Leverage
authors: Lifeng Gu; Dirk Hackbarth; Yuxin Luo
affiliations: Sy Syms School of Business, Yeshiva University, New York 10033; Questrom School of Business, Boston University, Boston, Massachusetts 02215; and European Corporate Governance Institute (ECGI), 1000 Brussels, Belgium; School of Finance, Renmin University of China, Beijing 100872, China
abstract: Firms’ inflexibility to adjust their scale persistently explains capital structure variations in a comprehensive sample and randomly selected subsamples. Higher inflexibility leads to lower financial leverage, potentially due to higher default risk and lower value of tax shields. Contraction inflexibility determines leverage more than expansion inflexibility. Moreover, our inflexibility measure explains financial leverage significantly better than other variables that potentially capture certain aspects of adjustment costs for capital or labor. In addition, inflexible firms increase leverage more following a positive credit supply shock. Analyses employing instrumental variables estimation confirm our main finding. Our results suggest inflexibility shapes corporate financial policies. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. title: Impact of Data Privacy Regulations on Recommender Systems Performance
authors: Liben Chen; Meizi Zhou; Yicheng Song; Gediminas Adomavicius
affiliations: University of Minnesota, Information and Decision Sciences, Minneapolis, Minnesota, United States; Boston University, Information Systems, Boston, Massachusetts, United States; university of minnesota, carlson school of management, minneapolis, Minnesota, United States
abstract: Data privacy regulations empower consumers to control the collection of their personal data. A significant consequence of these regulations is their effect on various data-driven business solutions, especially on personalization technologies and recommender systems. We investigate the potential impacts of diverse real-world data privacy practices (that can be adopted by firms in response to various data protection regulations) on the recommender systems performance. We also examine how these impacts vary across different personalization contexts and applications. In particular, we distinguish between scenarios where the user population exhibits more stable vs. more dynamic (i.e., changing) preferences, as these scenarios often represent distinctly different recommendation settings. We use a simulation framework, carefully seeded with real-world data, for a comprehensive evaluation of the recommender system performance under numerous scenarios, such as different recommendation algorithms, different data privacy practices, different degrees of users' preference dynamics, etc. Extensive computational experiments uncover several robust performance patterns for different data privacy practices and highlight substantial differences between recommendation settings with stable vs. changing user preferences. Furthermore, building upon the comprehensive findings from our computational experiments, we propose flexible, parameterizable data privacy practice designs based on the notion of revelation protection. The proposed approach is designed to provide an effective balance between personalization performance and privacy considerations, as demonstrated using extensive simulation experiments. The findings of this study have significant implications for the design of privacy-aware recommender systems in the context of contemporary data protection regulations. The findings can also be informative to policymakers for understanding the practical implications of various data privacy practices and for designing future policies.

title: A Moral Foundations Perspective on CEO Political Ideology
authors: Moritz Appels; Marc Kowalzick; Michael Woywode
affiliations: Erasmus University Rotterdam; University of Mannheim
abstract: As a reflection of their fundamental value systems, CEOs’ political ideology has come to be regarded as a major predictor of their strategic decision-making. Among the most persistent characterizations in this literature, liberal-leaning CEOs are considered to exhibit a distinct preference for evenhanded outcomes and pro-social corporate practices due to their ideological endorsement of equality—an association derived from the conceptualization of political ideologies along the motivated cognition perspective and routinely used to differentiate them from their more conservative peers. Yet, moral psychologists increasingly call for a broader understanding of the moral values differentiating liberals and conservatives. We therefore introduce moral foundations theory to the study of CEO political ideology, according to which liberal- and conservative-leaning CEOs differ in their focus on individual- versus group-centric concerns but, contrary to the existing consensus, should both endorse evenhanded outcomes and pro-social corporate practices. We find evidence for corresponding U-shaped rather than linear effects of CEOs’ political ideology in a sample of over 1,600 S&P 1500 CEOs. As such, we offer a novel theoretical perspective on CEOs’ political ideology and its organizational ramifications.

title: Competitive Dormancy in Interfirm Rivalry: Consequences for Rival Actions
authors: Tianxu Chen; Jianhong Chen; Lingling Pan; Wenpin Tsai; Ming-Jer Chen
affiliations: West Virginia University; University of New Hampshire; University of Pittsburgh; Pennsylvania State University; University of Virginia
abstract: In this study, we examine the implications of competitive dormancy, defined as a situation in which a focal firm’s observed time span of inaction following its prior action has exceeded the firm’s typical duration between successive actions. We argue that competitive dormancy may be perceived as inconsistent with a rival’s expectations and may be associated with an interpretive process concerning the rival’s subsequent actions. Integrating expectancy violation theory (EVT) and competitive dynamics research, we propose that the relationship between a focal firm’s competitive dormancy and the likelihood of rivals’ subsequent actions varies with their relative market standing and strategic resource commitment. Using a sample of 78,055 daily observations from 28 firms across 14 industries from 2000 to 2017, we find support for our hypotheses.

title: Systemic Risk Revisited: A Working Definition and Diagnostic Framework for Risk Analysis
authors: Jianping Yan; Jiahong Wen; Jiquan Zhang; Qinmian Bai
affiliations: Key Laboratory of Resilient Cities and Integrated Risk Management of Shanghai Emergency Management Bureau Shanghai Normal University Shanghai China; Rodel Risk Solutions Inc. Toronto Canada; School of Environment and Geographical Sciences Shanghai Normal University Shanghai China; School of Environment Northeast Normal University Changchun China; Jilin Province Science and Technology Innovation Center of Agro‐Meteorological Disaster Risk Assessment and Prevention Jilin Province Science and Technology Innovation Center of Agro‐Meteorological Disaster Risk Assessment and Prevention Changchun China
abstract: ABSTRACT Systemic risk has gained increasing attention across disaster risk reduction, climate governance, finance, infrastructure, and other domains, yet its meaning and application remain inconsistent. Existing definitions emphasize interdependence, contagion, complexity, uncertainty, cascading effects, and system‐wide disruption, but differ in analytical focus and operational use. This paper reviews major definitional traditions and argues that a working definition and diagnostic framework can clarify the analytical basis of systemic risk. We define systemic risk as potential damage, loss, and impact that propagate through interdependencies, feedbacks, and nonlinear processes within or across interconnected systems. Building on this definition, the paper develops a diagnostic framework based on system structure, propagation pathways, dynamic mechanisms, and cascading consequences. These dimensions help distinguish systemic risks from risks that are severe, complex, or large scale but remain relatively contained, and provide a structured basis for examining how adverse consequences propagate within and across interconnected systems in different domains.

title: An Agent‐Based Model for Post‐Disaster Resource Allocation Considering Dynamic Demand
authors: Xihui Wang; Wanting Shao; Yu Fan; Liang Liang
affiliations: School of Management University of Science and Technology of China Hefei China; Key Laboratory of Emergency Logistics and Relief Supply Provision Ministry of Emergency Management Langfang China; School of Safety Engineering Jiangxi University of Science and Technology Ganzhou China
abstract: ABSTRACT In the response phase of a disaster, effective and equitable resource allocation is critical for meeting the needs of affected populations and maintaining the social order in disaster‐stricken areas. However, dynamic demand driven by the mobility of disaster‐affected populations can substantially impact resource allocation outcomes. To consider this mobility in the resource allocation problem, in this paper, we employ an agent‐based model to simulate cross‐shelter movements and assess the performance of resource allocation strategies considering a gradual increase of total available resources over time. A novel resource allocation strategy is proposed, which leverages demand estimation through a machine learning (ML) method‐XGBoost. We then compare this approach against two conventional strategies: uniform distribution and historical data averaging. Through case studies using real‐world data of Typhoon Ragasa from Shenzhen in China and Lal‐lo in the Philippines, we demonstrate that our proposed strategy comprehensively outperforms the other two in terms of effectiveness, equity and stability. In conclusion, this ML‐based prediction approach offers valuable insights to support decision‐makers in the formulation of resource allocation plans.

title: Assessment of Risks, Efficiency, Costs, and Gain of Natural Hazard (Catastrophe) Consequences Prevention Based on Geophysical Monitoring
authors: Leonid F. Chernogor; Leonid L. Chornohor
affiliations: Department of Space Radio Physics V. N. Karazin Kharkiv National University Kharkiv Ukraine; Laboratory of Environmental Research, State Scientific Institution “Institute for Single Crystals” Kharkiv Ukraine
abstract: ABSTRACT The purpose of this paper is to quantitatively estimate the efficiency of forecasting hazards and catastrophic processes induced by high‐energy terrestrial sources, based on an integrated monitoring of the state of geophysical processes. Using methods of mathematical statistics and detection theory, relations have been obtained that can be used to calculate the coefficients of the efficiency of warning of catastrophes and the costs associated with a predicted event. The hazard (catastrophe) prevention efficiency coefficient has been shown to be dependent only on the conditional probability of missing a hazard. The relative cost parameter is a function of five parameters: a priori probability of the unwanted event, a conditional false alarm probability, a conditional missed detect probability, relative costs in the case of false alarm probability, and costs to minimize consequences of the hazardous event in case it has been accurately forecast. The gain from organizing geophysical monitoring has been estimated for a few dangers and catastrophes of terrestrial nature. The gain has been shown to be significant in many cases. An energy‐based classification of the most important natural sources of hazards and catastrophes, as well as their consequences, is proposed or improved.

title: Forecasting LLM‐Enabled Biorisk and the Efficacy of Safeguards
authors: Bridget Williams; Luca Righetti; Josh Rosenberg; Rebecca Ceppas de Castro; Otto Kuusela; Rhiannon Britt; Emily Soice; Alvaro Morales; Jon Sanders; Seth Donoughe; James Black; Ezra Karger; Philip E. Tetlock
affiliations: Forecasting Research Institute Claymont Delaware United States; Centre for the Governance of AI London United Kingdom; SecureBio Cambridge Massachusetts United States; Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security Baltimore Maryland United States; Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago Chicago Illinois United States; Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania Philadelphia Pennsylvania United States
abstract: ABSTRACT Capabilities of large language models (LLMs) on several biological benchmarks have prompted not only excitement about their usefulness for research but also concern about biosecurity risks. We recruited 46 subject‐matter experts in biology and biosecurity, and 22 generalist forecasters to estimate the risks of growing LLM capabilities. Most respondents expected some hypothetical LLM capabilities to increase their estimates of risk and dramatically underestimated the rate of LLM progress in those capabilities. When these capabilities arose, the median forecast did update as anticipated. The median expert initially predicted a 0.3% annual risk of a human‐caused epidemic that causes 100,000 deaths. This estimate then rose to 1.5% conditional on several hypothetical LLM capabilities, including matching the performance of a top‐performing team of virologists on a virology troubleshooting test, which the median expert did not expect to occur until 2030. Given this finding, we conducted a baselining study and found that LLMs already crossed this performance threshold in April 2025. A follow‐up survey conducted after these results were available found that forecasters significantly updated their median unconditional risk estimates upward, with the new median expert forecast of annual risk rising to 1.5% (as anticipated by the earlier conditional forecasts). More encouragingly, most experts thought that the adoption of LLM safeguards and mandatory nucleic acid screening would negate the risk associated with some hypothetical LLM capabilities.

title: Anticipating Surprises by Expanding a Risk Assessment's Possibility Space Into the Unknown With C – K Theory
authors: James Derbyshire
affiliations: Chester Business School University of Chester, Queen's Park Campus Chester UK
abstract: ABSTRACT What should a risk assessor do if she suspects the possibilities derivable from presently available knowledge are incomplete? Risk analysts often encounter this problem when assessing risk in open systems that produce novel outcomes leading to surprises. The solution is to expand the possibility space into the unknown. Yet the novel possibilities then included cannot be mere figments of the imagination; they must be tethered to presently available knowledge to be credible. This may seem paradoxical: to go beyond presently available knowledge by assessing novel possibilities, which, to be credible, must be grounded in presently available knowledge. Yet it is not quite as contradictory as it may first seem. C – K Theory (CKT) was developed to explain how innovators overcome a similar problem when designing a new product. An innovation involves creating something that has novel features. Some of its components may, therefore, not yet exist, and there may even be uncertainty about whether they are technically feasible. This lack of knowledge makes it difficult to determine the innovation's possibility space—a difficulty similar to that faced when assessing risks in open systems. CKT describes how innovators overcome this problem by iteratively moving between a knowledge space comprising established facts and decidable propositions and a conceptual space representing novel, as‐yet‐undecidable propositions. As illustrated herein using the cases of the credit crunch and the 9/11 terrorist attack, CKT can help anticipate surprises by generating, expanding, and integrating the possibility space within the extended ( C , U ) risk‐assessment framework.

title: Natural Is Not Necessarily Safer: A Probabilistic Assessment of Risk–Risk Trade‐Offs Between Cardiovascular and Genotoxic Effects of Food Preservatives
authors: Min‐Pei Ling; Ying‐Hsuan Lee
affiliations: Department of Food Science National Taiwan Ocean University Keelung City Taiwan
abstract: ABSTRACT To extend product shelf life, it is especially important to prevent foods from deteriorating. Apart from the traditional methods of adding salt or sugar in large amounts, other additives, such as food preservatives, can also be applied to achieve the aim of food preservation. This study employs probabilistic risk assessment (PRA) to quantify human health impacts associated with exposure to sodium chloride, sucrose, benzoic acid (BA), and sorbic acid (SA), utilizing cardiovascular disease (CVD) prevalence and micronuclei (MN) induction frequency as dual epidemiological and toxicological endpoints. We evaluated the risks of natural and artificial preservatives in products, such as pickled vegetables, fermented vegetables, candied fruits, and preserved fruits, with the same antibacterial efficiency and under controlled pH and water activity conditions. The results revealed a significant risk trade‐off: Although the CVD prevalence associated with natural preservatives reached 16.2%–18.2% across different food categories, the MN frequency induced by artificial preservatives remained comparatively lower at 7.4%–11.6%. The results suggest that combining natural and artificial preservatives may reduce sodium chloride or sucrose intake and the associated cardiovascular health risks compared with using natural preservatives alone. These findings indicate that although limiting high‐sodium and high‐sugar foods is crucial for cardiovascular health, dietary exposure to artificial preservatives, such as BA and SA, was associated with relatively low estimated genotoxic risks, though potential hepatic or renal impacts warrant further investigation.

title: Assessing the Relative Contribution of Pre‐Deployment Abroad Versus In‐Mission Dirofilaria immitis Infections in French Military Working Dogs Screened Post‐Mission: A Quantitative Risk Assessment
authors: Amélia Grosbois; Veronica Risco‐Castillo; Stéphanie Watier‐Grillot; Guillaume Crozet
affiliations: Laboratoire de Santé Animale EPIMIM Ecole Nationale Vétérinaire d'Alfort Anses Maisons‐Alfort France; 22e Groupe vétérinaire de Bordeaux Bordeaux France; Laboratoire de Santé Animale, BIPAR Anses, INRAE, Ecole Nationale Vétérinaire d'Alfort Maisons‐Alfort France; Biopôle Alfort Ecole Nationale Vétérinaire d'Alfort Maisons‐Alfort France; Groupe d'experts en épidémiologie animale Direction de la médecine des forces Tours France; Département Anticipation et Intervention Centre d’Épidémiologie et de Santé Publique des Armées Marseille France
abstract: ABSTRACT Dirofilaria immitis ( D. immitis ) is a mosquito‐borne nematode responsible for canine cardiopulmonary dirofilariasis, a parasitic infection widely distributed worldwide and established in mainland France, particularly in southern regions. Military working dogs (MWDs) may be at increased risk of exposure to vector‐borne pathogens because of their predominantly outdoor lifestyle and frequent missions abroad. Nevertheless, D. immitis infection remains sporadic in this population, likely due to well‐implemented medical prophylaxis. The aim of this study was to investigate the likely origin of D. immitis infections detected in MWD during post‐mission screening using a quantitative risk analysis approach. Scenario trees were developed to describe the sequences of events leading to the return of an infected dog from a mission abroad, accounting for parasite biology, prophylactic measures, and compliance. The model estimated a mean annual number of 4.25 infected MWD returning from missions out of an average annual population of 466 returning dogs, of which 79% were detected through post‐mission screening. Most infections were likely acquired before deployment, either during previous missions, at the breeding facility before purchase, or within mainland France. Only 7.9% of infections acquired during missions were expected to be detected by testing performed at the end of the post‐mission quarantine period. Alternative scenarios highlighted the effectiveness of chemoprophylaxis, as its absence was associated with a 3.2‐fold increase in the number of infected dogs. Simulations also showed that extending the interval between return and testing would substantially improve the detection of mission‐acquired infections. These findings support the continued use of preventive measures while questioning the adequacy of current post‐mission screening alone for identifying D. immitis infections acquired during deployment.

title: People, places, and firms: improving our understanding of wage and productivity disparities
authors: Yadira Gómez-Hernández; Henry G Overman
affiliations: Brunel Centre, University of Bath , Bath, BA2 7AY,; Centre for Economic Performance, London School of Economics , London, WC2A 2AE,; Department of Geography and Environment, London School of Economics , London, WCA 2AE,; Centre for Economic Policy Research , 187 boulevard Saint-Germain , Paris, 75007,
abstract: Abstract In many countries spatial disparities in wages and productivity are large and persistent. This raises questions about the causes and consequences of such disparities. Two inter-related issues—the sorting of high skilled workers and the productivity benefits of urban density—are central to the way in which urban economists have approached these questions. In this commentary, we argue that despite the emerging consensus that sorting matters for wage disparities, the literature has made less progress on other dimensions of these disparities and a number of methodological issues remain unresolved.

title: Every Mile Counts: Geographical Distance as Administrative Burden in Intellectual Property Services
authors: Shenghua Lu
affiliations: Zhejiang University Assistant Professor, School of Public Affairs,
abstract: Abstract While existing research has examined procedural and informational sources of administrative burden, this paper examines how organizational design choices about the geographic location of administrative authority institutionalize spatial burdens on firms. We leverage China's decentralization reform in trademark registration services as a natural experiment to test this theory. This reform reduced geographic distance by establishing local acceptance windows across the country from 2016 to 2019. Prior to this reform, trademark applications had to be submitted exclusively at the centralized Beijing office, imposing substantial geographic barriers on firms nationwide. Using a unique dataset covering over 37 million trademark applications from 294 Chinese cities, we employ a staggered difference-in-differences approach to estimate the causal effects of reduced geographic distance on trademark filings. We find that establishing local acceptance windows increased trademark applications by approximately 4.4 percent, or roughly 209,000 additional filings in 2019 alone. Moreover, the reform generated compound distributional outcomes: small and medium-sized enterprises responded more strongly than larger firms, and the new applicants drawn into the trademark system were concentrated in cities with thinner infrastructure. Mechanism analysis confirms that this increase is primarily driven by distance reduction rather than improvements in administrative efficiency or reductions in corruption. The findings provide large-scale causal evidence on the behavioral consequences of redistributing administrative service delivery across space, demonstrating that physical accessibility remains crucial for equitable service uptake even amid the digital transformation of administrative services.

title: Detecting Careless Responding: A Comparison of Norm Group-Based Mahalanobis Distance and Norm Group-Based Person-Total Correlation with Their Sample-Based Counterparts
authors: Philippe Goldammer; Yannik A. Escher; Peter Lucas Stöckli; Hubert Annen; Anna Luca Heimann
affiliations: Military Academy at ETH Zurich; School of Management and Technology, Leuphana University Lüneburg; University of Surrey
abstract: Detecting careless responding in self-report questionnaires has gained considerable attention. Different detection methods have been proposed, with implicit methods offering clear advantages over explicit ones. Mahalanobis distance (MD) and person-total correlation ( r pbis ) are among the most promising implicit detection methods. However, previous research has suggested that MD and r pbis are less accurate indicators of careless responding when the percentage of careless respondents in the sample is high and that norm group-based (NGB) MD and r pbis might be more accurate alternatives under that condition. In two simulation studies and a reanalysis of real data, we examined whether NGB MD and NGB r pbis indeed outperform their sample-based (SB) counterparts in a variety of careless responding patterns. The three main findings were as follows: (1) NGB MD outperformed SB MD in most conditions in three studies, (2) both MD indices (but not r pbis indices) were ineffective when simulated scale-midpoint invariant and full straightlining careless responding had to be detected, and (3) NGB r pbis almost never outperformed SB r pbis . We therefore recommend using NGB MD instead of SB MD, and using SB r pbis instead of NGB r pbis when screening data for careless responding.

title: EXPRESS: A Learning and Searching Method for Integrated Process Planning and Scheduling
authors: Hongpei Li; Han Zhang; Ziyan He; Jiaqi Hu; Hongsong Yuan
abstract: The integrated process planning and scheduling problem combines process route planning and shop scheduling to achieve high efficiency in manufacturing and maximize resource utilization, which is crucial for modern manufacturing systems. Traditional approaches, such as mixed-integer linear programming and heuristic algorithms, often struggle to balance solution quality and computational efficiency, particularly in large-scale scenarios. To address this, we propose learning-then-searching, an efficient framework combining deep reinforcement learning with heuristic search to solve integrated process planning and scheduling problems. We formulate the problem as a Markov decision process and develop a deep reinforcement learning method tailored to capture the complex relationships among operations, machines, and jobs. With the learned policy distributions, Monte Carlo tree search employs learned priors and problem-specific rollouts to further refine scheduling strategies, effectively balancing exploration and exploitation to achieve better solutions. Experimental results show that the proposed framework improves solution efficiency and quality over traditional methods across benchmark and large-scale instances, with pronounced advantages when route ambiguity is high. It also offers practitioners a flexible tradeoff between rapid policy-based decisions and further refinement through tree search when additional computation time is available.

title: EXPRESS: Bridging the Gap: The Impact of Online Booking of Healthcare Appointments Service
authors: Liuyi He; Jifeng Luo; Panpan Wang; Zhiyan Wu; Han Zhang
abstract: Online healthcare communities (OHCs) play an important role in transforming healthcare delivery. While existing literature has primarily focused on the impact of teleconsultation services on offline demand, the influence of integrating offline access into OHCs on teleconsultation remains largely unexplored. This study addresses the gap by investigating how the integration of offline access into OHCs affects the utilization of teleconsultation services. We leverage a natural experiment in an OHC involving the implementation of the Online Booking of Healthcare Appointments (OBHA) feature, which allows patients to secure in-person visit appointments in the OHC. Using difference-in-differences (DID) models, we find a significant increase in new demand for adopter physicians’ teleconsultation services following the integration of OBHA, without deterioration in service quality. Notably, the increased demand largely comes from patients in remote and underserved areas seeking consultations with high-quality physicians, exhibiting a cascading effect. Furthermore, we find that OBHA adoption extends the geographic reach of physicians’ teleconsultation services and promotes a more equitable distribution of teleconsultation utilization across regions. Our findings indicate that integrating offline access into OHCs not only boosts the utilization of teleconsultation services but also helps reduce health disparities by facilitating access to high-quality resources. This study contributes to the literature on healthcare operations management, healthcare information technology, and health disparities. The insights gleaned from the study also offer practical suggestions to policymakers, OHC operators, physicians, and patients.

title: EXPRESS: Simplifying the Madness of Multiple Entries in March Madness
authors: Jeff Decary; David Bergman; Carlos Cardonha; Jason Imbrogno; Andrea Lodi
abstract: Multi-entry betting pools for single-elimination tournaments create a portfolio-design problem: a participant may submit several brackets whose scores are highly dependent, while payouts are typically concentrated on the best-performing entry. Motivated by March Madness pools, we study the problem of selecting a portfolio of brackets that maximizes the expected maximum score (EMS) across entries. This objective captures the top-heavy nature of such contests without requiring a model of opponents' bracket choices, which is difficult to estimate reliably in a tournament played only once per year. We first establish computational and structural properties of the EMS objective. Exact EMS evaluation is #P-hard in general, although it is polynomial-time computable for any fixed number of entries with an exponent that grows with the portfolio size. For two entries, EMS decomposes into single-entry expected-score terms and an expected absolute score-gap term, making explicit the trade-off between selecting individually strong brackets and diversifying across outcomes. These insights motivate two sample average approximation algorithms: an entry-by-entry method based on marginal EMS contributions and a round-by-round method that exploits the geometrically increasing scoring weights in March Madness by emphasizing late-round diversification. Computational experiments using historical tournament data show that the round-by-round method scales reliably and outperforms direct SAA and an entropy-based benchmark for larger portfolios. In a real high-stakes DraftKings pool from the 2023 tournament, our 100-entry portfolio would have achieved a 2.54% probability of attaining a maximum-scoring entry, with higher expected profit than the portfolios submitted by several elite professional bettors.

title: EXPRESS: Coevolution of Trader Similarity Networks and Follower Dynamics in Social Trading
authors: Ye Liu; Mingwen Yang; Yong Tan
abstract: Social trading platforms have been gaining popularity against traditional brokerages over the past few years. Compared with traders on traditional financial markets, those on social trading platforms often exhibit more similar trading strategies. In this paper, we examine the impact of strategy similarity patterns on traders' popularity. We identify two competing effects of similarity: a substitution effect, whereby traders with similar strategies become interchangeable and compete for followers; and a social proof effect, whereby similarity signals credibility in an environment characterized by high uncertainty and limited verifiable credentials, thereby attracting followers. To empirically examine these effects, we construct a dynamic similarity network and develop a coevolution model that captures the joint evolution of network structure and follower dynamics. Using data from a leading social trading platform, we find that, on average, greater similarity leads to a decline in a trader’s followers over time, indicating that the substitution effect dominates. Importantly, this relationship is heterogeneous. For more established traders, the substitution effect is stronger, such that greater similarity reduces their popularity. In contrast, for less established traders, the social proof effect dominates, and similarity increases their popularity. Using counterfactual simulations, we show that reducing the density of the similarity network and promoting a more balanced distribution of followers can mitigate the negative substitution effect, thereby increasing the total number of followers on the platform and, consequently, the platform revenue. Our study identifies several managerial and operational implications for the social trading platforms.

title: EXPRESS: The Role of Ease-of-Return Experience on Contingent Free Shipping Policies
authors: Ashish Kabra; Wedad J. Elmaghraby; Nitish Jain
abstract: Contingent free shipping (CFS) policies, whereby consumers get free shipping if their orders exceed a certain amount, are commonplace. Such a policy aims to nudge customers to place larger orders by adding additional items and/or buying more expensive items ( order-swelling ). A less desirable possible outcome is that customers pad their orders to avoid paying the shipping fee but later return the opportunistic or impulse-purchase items ( return-swelling ). A retailer designing the CFS policy’s terms—threshold and shipping fee—should balance these competing effects. We study how the retailer's return environment, specifically the ease-of-return experience (EOR) for customers, moderates order-swelling or return-swelling behavior induced by a CFS policy. We collaborate with an online fashion retailer that switched across multiple CFS policies over time and offered home pickup of returns in some markets but not in others. Our difference-in-differences empirical strategy builds on these policy switches and the location-based variation in the EOR. We find that the EOR can considerably impact the relative profit performance of the CFS policies and that it moderates both the order-swelling and the return-swelling responses. Our counterfactual analysis reveals that return-swelling is the key driver of the observed difference in the relative profit performance of CFS policies across the two EOR market types. Our study documents a novel determinant of the financial performance of a CFS policy: the ease-of-return experience. Our analysis indicates that our collaborating retailer would be better off selecting a (relatively) lenient CFS policy in more convenient EOR markets and a (relatively) stringent CFS policy in less convenient EOR markets.

title: EXPRESS: Revitalizing the Grocery Store Experience: An Empirical Study on the Spillover Effects of Experiential Services
authors: Bengü Nur Özdemir; Stanley Frederick W. T. Lim
abstract: Grocery retailers increasingly use experiential services to attract customers to their stores. However, it remains unclear whether these services generate positive spillover effects to core grocery sales or cannibalize existing demand. We provide the first empirical evidence by studying a grocery retailer that introduced a taphouse as its first experiential service and examining the underlying mechanisms. We combine store transaction records with SafeGraph's point-of-interest data and survey data on product attributes. Using a quasi-experimental design, we specify a synthetic difference-in-differences estimator with staggered treatment timings. Our results show significant positive spillover effects. On average, stores that feature a taphouse experienced a 5.97% increase in daily sales volume, a 6.82% rise in sales revenue, a 5.76% increase in transactions, and a 6.18% expansion in product variety compared to stores without a taphouse. Our mechanism analyses suggest that these results are associated with activity through both extensive (newly observed customers) and intensive (greater purchasing activity among existing customers) margins. We find that an average order contains fewer but relatively higher-priced items, leaving average order value statistically unchanged. Newly acquired customers make relatively smaller purchases than existing customers, whose order size does not change significantly following the taphouse introduction. We also find that products complementary to the taphouse and those with a greater propensity for impulse purchasing account for larger shares of grocery sales following taphouse introduction. Finally, nearby competing supermarkets experience reductions in both total visits and unique visitors, suggesting that local competitive substitution may contribute to the observed customer expansion. To assess generalizability, we replicate the analysis with another grocery chain in a different region that introduced a full restaurant and obtain qualitatively similar results. Overall, the findings indicate that adding a taphouse can effectively increase grocery sales volume and revenue. Although high setup costs may deter adoption, our break-even analysis projects recovery in approximately 34 to 39 weeks from grocery-side gross-margin contributions alone, or 27 to 44 weeks when alternative assumptions about taphouse profitability, including operating losses, are incorporated.

title: Reconfiguring external and internal networks for resilience, agility and ambidexterity under geopolitical volatility
authors: Umair Tanveer; Thinh Gia Hoang; Shamaila Ishaq; Stefan Gold
affiliations: Business School, University of Exeter–Streatham Campus , ,; Ho Chi Minh City University of Economics and Finance(UEF) , ,; Derby International Business School, University of Derby , ,; TUM Campus Straubing for Biotechnology and Sustainability, Technical University of Munich , ,
abstract: Purpose Geopolitical tensions and economic policy volatility are compelling multinational firms to redesign both external supply chain networks and their intra-organisational networks of plants, subsidiaries and governance. This study examines how intra-organisational networks are redesigned in response to geopolitically induced reshaping of external supply chain networks and how this redesign enables resilience, agility and ambidexterity. Design/methodology/approach The study uses a qualitative multiple-case design with three longitudinal focal cases and five supporting cases. The data comprise 58 semi-structured interviews, supplemented by secondary documents to reconstruct case trajectories over time. Findings Geopolitically driven external network reshaping heightens dependence and power asymmetry through concentrated bottlenecks, low substitutability, and compliance-gated access. Firms respond through buffering, bridging, and selective internalisation, but these moves become effective only when internal decision rights, subsidiary mandates, and integration capacity are redesigned. Originality/value The study conceptualises external and intra-organisational network restructuring as a coupled, dependence-driven process under geopolitical volatility. It extends Resource Dependence Theory by showing that dependence-management strategies require internal re-architecture to become executable, thereby reframing resilience, agility, and ambidexterity as outcomes of organisational redesign rather than static capabilities.

title: Interesting and impactful research avenues emerge from teaching operations management
authors: Tyson R. Browning
affiliations: Neeley School of Business, Texas Christian University , , ,
abstract: Purpose This article reflects on how teaching operations management (OM) to graduate students and executives provides a rich source of interesting and impactful OM research avenues. Design/methodology/approach While it is common to hear that the latest research should keep teaching fresh and relevant, this article flips this advice to discuss interesting and impactful OM research topics emerging from the challenges of teaching an MBA core course. Findings This article suggests six avenues for future research that emerged from teaching – how company operations pertain to its strategy, the role of chief operating officer (COO), enterprise processes, process improvement, performance measurement, and automation/artificial intelligence (AI) – and specific research questions within each avenue. Research limitations/implications The proposed research questions are exemplary and not comprehensive. Practical implications Addressing the proposed research questions will lead to interesting, practically relevant and impactful results. Social implications Addressing the proposed research questions will lead to socially relevant and impactful results. Originality/value This article reverses the typical admonition to let research inform teaching, showing how considering the counter-relationship illuminates interesting and impactful research avenues.

title: The Role of Institutions in the Relationship Between Informal Competition and New Product Development in Emerging Economies
authors: Sadrac Cenophat; Martin Eisend
affiliations: EM Strasbourg Business School Université de Strasbourg Strasbourg France; The University of Vienna Wien Austria
abstract: ABSTRACT Academic Summary Research has argued that informal competition (IC)—the competitive pressure from firms that are unregistered but derive income from the production of legal goods and services—increases formal (i.e., legally registered) firms' engagement in new product development (NPD) in emerging economies. However, other studies have suggested that IC may decrease such engagement. Drawing on an institutional perspective, we argue that the relationship between IC and NPD is contingent on the level of IC and the influence of formal and informal institutions. A multilevel analysis of 29,520 formal firms across 21 emerging economies indicates an inverted U‐shaped relationship between IC and NPD probability. Low to moderate levels of IC increase NPD probability, whereas higher levels reduce it. The findings also reveal that this relationship varies across emerging economies, with significant cross‐level interactions between IC and elements of formal (e.g., regulatory control, availability of finance) and informal institutions (e.g., survival vs. self‐expression and traditional vs. secular‐rational values) shaping NPD probability. Managerial Summary Informal competition can stimulate formal firms' new product development at low to moderate levels, but high levels of IC can discourage it. Because informal firms spur innovation among their formal counterparts, policymakers should not automatically seek to eliminate IC. Instead, they should consider IC as a changing condition and adapt enforcement to its intensity. At low to moderate levels of IC, minimal enforcement may be appropriate as the innovation and consumer benefits associated with IC may outweigh its costs. As IC becomes more intense and begins to undermine formal firms' NPD, policymakers can tighten enforcement while offering informal firms incentives to formalize. For managers, the findings suggest that the strategic response to IC should also depend on its intensity. When IC is low, formal firms may continue to innovate despite financial constraints; managers can therefore pursue low‐risk, affordable products using frugal innovation methods, while policymakers can support these efforts through improved access to finance. Managers are also well‐advised to consider the institutional context. Unlike their counterparts in countries leaning toward survival values (e.g., India), formal firms operating in societies that lean toward self‐expression values (e.g., Uruguay) are more likely to engage in NPD when IC is low; the probability decreases as IC becomes higher.

title: HOW AND WHY CHANGE AGENTS LEVERAGE AMBIGUITY: DIGITAL CHANGE AS A PROGRESSION OF PROCESS CONFIGURATIONS
authors: Jonny Holmstrom; Kalle Lyytinen; Daniel Nylen; Viktor Arvidsson
affiliations: Umea Universitet; Case Western Reserve University; Linköping University
abstract: Digital change (DC) broadly entails a radical reconfiguration of an organization’s modus operandi through the deployment of a growing and often untried set of digital technologies. Prior research has extensively examined DC in terms of outcomes, antecedents, and mechanisms. However, one critical aspect remains underexplored: the role of ambiguity arising from unknown technologies, non-linear change processes, and the coexistence of multiple organizational goals. Existing DC literature commonly attributes failure to an inability to remove ambiguity – that is, the contested and fluid meanings, goals, and means of DC – and to align clear strategic intent with well-defined technology functions. We challenge this view by conceptualizing ambiguity not as a problem to be eliminated, but as an inherent and generative condition of DC that must be actively reckoned with. Drawing on March’s distinction between goal ambiguity and technology ambiguity, we develop a framework of four DC configurations based on the presence or absence of ambiguity in strategic intent and in the articulated role of digital technologies. We analyze four DC cases, treating each as a progression through shifting configurations of goal and technology ambiguity. Using three longitudinal empirical cases and one baseline alignment case from prior literature, we identify four distinct DC pathways, each characterized by a specific sequence of configurations. We theorize how ambiguity shapes DC trajectories and outcomes and show that practitioners may need to deliberately increase or decrease ambiguity in goals and/or technology functions to propel DC forward.

title: Responsible Management Education and Its Potential as an Epistemic Object of Change
authors: Valtteri A. Aaltonen; Marjo E. Siltaoja
affiliations: Department of Environmental Sciences, Faculty of Biological and Environmental Sciences University of Helsinki Helsinki Finland; Management and Leadership Jyväskylä University School of Business and Economics Jyväskylä Finland
abstract: Abstract This study examines whether and how RME can be performed as an epistemic object to broaden business schools’ education on climate change. The research builds on a qualitative case study involving 10 Finnish business schools. The analysis reveals that RME is performed as both an epistemic object and a boundary object, with different implications for its embeddedness within institutions. Our findings show how accreditations have introduced RME as a boundary object enforcing performativity around sustainability themes yet enabling disciplines to maintain their distinct or limited roles. At the same time, RME is met with both resistance and compliance, depending on how well the object fits with disciplinary boundaries and career trajectories. Lastly, as an epistemic object, RME encourages co‐reflexivity, which is essential for climate‐proofing business schools. We discuss the possibilities of a hybrid orientation of RME as both a boundary object and an epistemic object for enforcing climate‐orientation in management education.

title: Harnessing Power Through External Collaborative Innovation: How Incumbent Inventors Navigate Rising Talent Influx in Developed‐country MNE Subsidiaries
authors: Tianjiao Xia; Xiaohui Liu
affiliations: Norwich Business School University of East Anglia Norwich UK; Birmingham Business School University of Birmingham Birmingham UK
abstract: Abstract This paper examines how, and under what conditions, the increasing presence of highly skilled local employees (HSLEs) within subsidiaries of developed‐country multinational enterprises (DCMNEs) influences incumbent local inventors’ external collaborative innovation. Adopting a power dependence perspective, we propose that incumbent local inventors are more likely to engage in external than internal collaborative innovation in response to the increasing presence of HSLEs. Successful external collaborative innovation enhances incumbent local inventors’ bargaining power by enabling them to gain stronger positions within external networks critical to DCMNEs’ innovation and to access alternative employment opportunities. We further contend that the positive relationship between the increasing presence of HSLEs and incumbent local inventors’ external collaborative innovation is strengthened by the boundary‐spanning characteristics of the management hierarchies, such as cross‐cultural CEOs and interlocking directors. Our analysis of DCMNE subsidiaries operating in China provides empirical support for these predictions. This research offers novel and important insights into collaborating‐by‐hiring, highlighting the increasing presence of HSLEs as a competitive mechanism for interorganizational collaborative innovation and emphasizing the strategic importance of externally leveraging the knowledge and expertise of incumbent inventors.

title: How Assumptions About Time Divide and Connect Epistemic Communities in Business and Management
authors: Stephanie Decker
affiliations: University of Birmingham Birmingham UK
abstract: Abstract Business and management studies comprise distinct epistemic communities that frequently do not interact or collaborate. While this has been explained as paradigm incommensurability, construct ambiguity or the variance–process, this CrossRoads article sets out a less commonly invoked source of difference: how our theories conceptualize time. This includes assumptions about whether the future is determined or open (temporal openness), whether and how change takes place (temporal directionality) and the appropriate timescales and detail for analysis (temporal duration). To illustrate the importance of these three temporal dimensions, influential traditions in strategy, entrepreneurship, institutional theory, process studies, population ecology, real‐options and scenario planning are mapped. The mapping demonstrates that many temporal differences between epistemic communities are differences of degree that may offer productive tensions for collaborative approaches, even though some may remain difficult to reconcile. Through a set of diagnostic questions, this CrossRoads piece offers a framework for interdisciplinary temporal brokerage within and beyond business and management.

title: Digitalization and Cybersecurity: Firm‐level Evidence
authors: Jukka Sihvonen
affiliations: University of Vaasa Vaasa Finland
abstract: Abstract Digitalization has opposing effects on cybersecurity: While new digital technologies can strengthen security capabilities, they simultaneously expand potential attack surfaces. To determine which effect dominates, we analyse 9606 US firm‐years (2006–2023) with 543 documented breaches and find that increased digitalization, measured through 10‐K business descriptions, significantly raises the likelihood of future cyber breaches. A one‐standard‐deviation increase in digitalization corresponds to up to a 10 percentage point higher breach probability, driven primarily by organizational rather than technological dimensions. Expert auditors and cybersecurity disclosure reduce breach likelihood, but their protective effect attenuates as digitalization rises; that of board and C‐suite technology expertise instead strengthens. These findings qualify the protective role of conventional monitoring in highly digitalized firms and point to a repositioning of cybersecurity governance from external monitoring towards digital expertise embedded in strategic decision‐making.

title: Unmanagement Education for the Age of Climate Crisis
authors: Fernanda Cassab Carreira; Isleide Arruda Fontenelle
affiliations: FGV EAESP Av. Nove de Julho, 2029, Bela Vista São Paulo 01313–902 Brazil
abstract: Abstract This paper examines how embodied, situated and relational experiences outside‐the‐classroom can open space for epistemic dislocations in Management Education under conditions of ecological crisis. Drawing on a qualitative pedagogical experience in a sustainability course in Brazil, informed by Design‐Based Research—whose assumptions of control, design and predictability we critically question–we explore conditions under which radical imaginaries may emerge through such experiences. Students engaged in encounters with human and non‐human others that generated discomfort and tension with habitual ways of knowing, opening possibilities for the emergence of (dis)enchanted imaginaries of Nature and (de)colonial imaginaries. These dynamics were intensified through situated and embodiment engagements, which at times gave rise to epistemic dislocations, or moments in which established ways of knowing lose their capacity to organize experience as alternative imaginaries become available. Those dislocations created temporary openings for participants to re‐examine their understandings of Nature, coloniality and socio‐ecological relations, remaining susceptible to reabsorption into dominant managerial frames. We contribute to climate‐oriented pedagogy by introducing Unmanagement Education, a reflexive pedagogical approach grounded in non‐mastery, embodiment and situated relationality, that may unsettle instituted imaginaries, opening space for epistemic dislocations to emerge under conditions of ecological crisis.

title: Teaching for Wonder: Pedagogical Openings for Epistemic Change in the Climate Crisis
authors: Chloe Preece; Pilar Rojas‐Gaviria; Emma Surman
affiliations: ESCP Business School 527 Finchley Road London NW3 7BG UK; Kedge Business School 680 Cr de la Libération Talence 33405 France; Birmingham Business School University House, Edgbaston Park Road Birmingham B15 2TY UK
abstract: Abstract The accelerating climate crisis demands profound changes in how management learning and education prepares students to engage with uncertainty and ecological interdependence. While recent scholarship calls for epistemic transformation in business schools, there is limited understanding of how pedagogy might cultivate the orientations required for such change. This paper advances wonder as a critical yet under‐theorized pedagogical orientation for climate‐responsive management education. We conceptualize wonder as an epistemic–affective orientation of attentional widening and humility in response to the more‐than‐known, capable of disrupting instrumental habits of knowing and sustaining openness to uncertainty. Drawing on an interpretive qualitative study of an arts‐based pedagogical collaboration with the Birmingham Royal Ballet, we develop a processual framework comprising five interrelated moments: encounter, suspension, engagement, refiguration and return. Together, these moments show how wonder reshapes students’ relationships to knowledge, enabling them to engage with complexity beyond instrumental frames. In doing so, the paper provides an empirically grounded theorization of wonder as a pedagogical mechanism for epistemic transformation and advances debates on what climate‐responsive management education could look like.

authors: Amrita Dhillon; Grammateia Kotsialou; Dilip Ravindran; Dimitrios Xefteris
affiliations: King's College London and CIAS Budapest Hungary; King's College London UK; Humboldt University of Berlin Berlin Germany; University of Cyprus Nicosia Cyprus
abstract: ABSTRACT Liquid democracy (LD) combines elements of direct and representative democracy: voters can either vote directly or delegate their votes to others. We study its information aggregation properties in a setting with heterogeneously and privately informed independent and partisan voters. We establish that LD always has equilibria that improve welfare and information aggregation relative to direct democracy, identify economically interpretable conditions under which these gains are strict, and characterise optimal delegation for salient classes of committees. However, while delegation improves the best‐equilibrium, it can also introduce robust inefficient equilibria that perform worse than direct democracy.

authors: CHRISTOPH HUBER; FELIX HOLZMEISTER; MAGNUS JOHANNESSON; CHRISTIAN KÖNIG‐KERSTING; ANNA DREBER; JÜRGEN HUBER; MICHAEL KIRCHLER
abstract: ABSTRACT Experimental asset markets provide a controlled approach to studying financial markets. We attempt to replicate 17 key results from four prominent studies, collecting new data from 166 markets with 1,544 participants. Only three of the 14 original results reported as statistically significant were successfully replicated. We fail to replicate findings on emotions, self‐control, and gender differences in bubble formation but confirm that experience reduces bubbles and cognitive skills explain trading success. Our study demonstrates the importance of replications in enhancing the credibility of scientific results in this field.

abstract: Abstract This paper highlights racial and ethnic preferences in corporate director elections. Using a comprehensive dataset of mutual fund voting records, we discover that mutual fund managers are more likely to vote for director nominees who share their racial or ethnic identity. Funds managed by White-dominated teams exhibit the strongest same-race preferences, particularly those in fund families with scarce minority representation. Same-race voting preferences have detrimental implications for the career outcomes of minority director candidates, and are associated with worse fund performance primarily when fund managers operate under weaker accountability. We investigate various potential mechanisms—including statistical discrimination, value maximization, conflicts of interest, social networks, and taste-based biases—and find that the evidence aligns most closely with a taste-based explanation for same-race preferential voting.
